instructions:
You are reading the plain-language text of a codebase map. A reader meets each field ALONE, inside one box, with no paragraph around it, and does not read code.

Judge ONLY these two things:
  1. UNKNOWN WORD — a term the reader has not met and the field does not explain. Product words and words already in the map's Glossary are fine; jargon, an internal codename, or an unexplained abbreviation is not.
  2. LOST PRECISION — the sentence is short and plain but says nothing specific. "The system checks the user" is the shape: grammatical, readable, and it names no decision, no data and no actor. This is the worse failure, because it looks correct.

Do NOT report sentence length, em dashes, code names or an opening "It" — those are counted deterministically and the lead already has the numbers.
Be conservative. Report a field only when you can say WHICH word is unknown, or WHAT the sentence should have said. If in doubt, pass the field.

For each field you flag, return its `where` exactly as given, one of `unknown word` or `lost precision`, and one short line naming the word or the missing specific.

fields.text: An advisory never stops a build; only a gate does.
A build stopped by a matter of judgement teaches its author to ignore every finding the tools print.
A build is clean only when every gate ran and no advisory is left open.
A gate that was skipped would read as a gate that passed, hiding a broken map behind a green report.
An advisory the operator decides to live with is silenced only by a reason recorded in the map.
Without one place to record the reason, the same advisory fires on every build until people stop reading.
A recorded reason is refused unless it names a finding the checks really read.
An operator would believe an advisory was answered while it keeps firing, and nothing would say so.
Every advisory a recorded reason silenced is still counted out loud in the build's report.
A silence nobody can see reads the same as having no findings, so a map can look clean by suppression.
A finding whose only honest answer is a fix cannot be silenced by a recorded reason.
An escape here would let a map record its own gaps as acceptable, which the checks exist to stop.
An advisory must say where the operator records the reason for living with it.
An advisory with nowhere to answer it is waved through forever, so the check changes nothing.
A run refuses to read or overwrite coyodex's own map unless the operator declares coyodex is the project being mapped.
A shell standing in the wrong folder reads a healthy result about the wrong product, or overwrites the accepted map.
Only files git accounts for are analysed, so ignored and generated trees stay out of the map.
Reading everything on disk fills the map with built output and copied libraries, and hides the product's real size.
A project's own exclusion patterns are named on every run, each beside the number of files it removed.
An over broad pattern hides a real gap from the very checks whose job is finding gaps.
A build never opens the map it is replacing, so the new map cannot quietly copy the old one.
Two maps agree because one copied the other, and nobody can tell copying from real agreement.
A map is built again from scratch only when the person asks, because a rebuild discards the accepted map.
A silent rebuild throws away every hand correction and the record of which code version the map described.
A correction only lasts where the build reads from, because every file the build produces is written again from scratch.
A repair everybody believes landed quietly disappears, and the same work is done again months later.
A warning the person decides to accept is silenced only by a note written under a heading the checks read.
A note nobody reads leaves the same warning arriving every run, so the real warnings get waved through.
A map names the version of the code it describes. That name is marked when the code on disk was never committed.
Unmarked, the map claims a committed version it does not describe. Every later comparison then misses the edits already baked in.
Lists a project's files, and reads any file exactly as it stood at the map's pinned commit.
Holds every project's map folder, the tool's own environment, and the remembered list of projects.
Opens and draws the map viewer page for a person on this machine.
Receives a file and a line from the map, so a person opens that exact spot in their editor.
Shows a mapped file on the web, pinned to the commit the map was built at.
Runs the installed skill that drives a map build, and names the conversation a build is stamped with.
Serves the two drawing libraries the viewer page loads in the browser.
Draws every diagram on the viewer page from the text the tool generates.
Lets a person pan and zoom a drawn diagram in the viewer.
Reads symbols and imports out of source files in many languages during the first pass.
